# How to Write AI Prompts That Look Like Real Polaroid Photos

> **In short:** AI image generators can produce convincing Polaroid-style photos, but most attempts come out looking like a clean digital frame around a sharp modern picture. The fix is in your prompt: name the camera and film stock, describe the lighting, add a few real-film imperfections, and use the right shape.

If you've ever typed "Polaroid photo" into an AI image tool and gotten back something that looks more like a phone snapshot with a white border, you're not alone. The reason is simple — the AI knows what a Polaroid *frame* looks like, but it doesn't automatically know what real Polaroid *film* looks like.

The good news is that the gap between "white border around a sharp photo" and "this could have come out of a 1985 Polaroid camera" is mostly a **prompt** problem. A prompt is just the instruction you give the AI. And prompts are something you can fix in five minutes.

## What you need before you start

You need a **text-to-image AI** — a tool that turns your written description into a picture. Popular options include ChatGPT's image generator, Midjourney, Google's image tools in Gemini, and open-source options like Stable Diffusion. The exact wording varies a little between them, but the building blocks below work across all of them.

You don't need a paid plan for this — free tiers usually handle it. Pick a subject first: a person, pet, place, or object you want to see "printed on film."

## Step 1 — Name the camera, not just the look

The first thing most people get wrong is describing only the result: "Polaroid photo of a cat." That tells the AI the *shape* of the image, not how it was *made*. The fix is to mention the camera and film stock by name, so the AI pulls from its knowledge of how that specific equipment behaves.

**What to type**: Start your prompt with the camera and film. Phrases like "shot on a Polaroid 600," "Polaroid SX-70," or "Instax Mini" all work. Add the film type if you can — "Polaroid 600 film," "Instax Mini film," "expired Polaroid from 1998."

**What you'll see**: Slightly softer focus, more natural color, and lighting that feels less like a studio shot.

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Polaroid 600 film photo of my golden retriever sitting on a worn couch, afternoon light from a window"

**You'll know it worked when** the colors look a touch faded and the lighting feels natural instead of crisp.

## Step 2 — Describe the light, not just the scene

Real Polaroids depend heavily on the light that hit them when the shutter clicked. Flash-heavy Polaroids look completely different from natural-light ones, and the film especially struggles with backlight and low light. The AI knows this if you tell it.

**What to type**: Add a lighting phrase. Options include "natural daylight," "overcast afternoon," "on-camera flash," "golden hour," "indoor tungsten light," or "dimly lit room." For that nostalgic feel, "soft window light" or "late afternoon sun" tends to work well.

**What you'll see**: Warmer or cooler tones, softer shadows, occasional flash glare if you asked for it.

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Polaroid 600 film photo of two friends laughing at a kitchen table, harsh on-camera flash, 1989"

**You'll know it worked when** the lighting feels like a real photograph from a specific moment rather than a generic product shot.

## Step 3 — Add the small imperfections

This is where most prompts succeed or fail. A "perfect" Polaroid looks fake because real instant film is never perfect. It has subtle quirks: uneven color, light leaks at the edges, slight chemical smudging, a soft **vignette** (a darker ring around the corners), and sometimes a thumbprint on the white border.

**What to type**: Build these into the prompt. Useful phrases include "slight color shift," "soft vignette," "light leak on the left edge," "slightly overexposed," "warm yellow tint," "faded colors," "a small thumbprint on the border," or "chemical bleed at the bottom." Pick two or three. Listing all of them at once makes the AI go overboard.

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Polaroid SX-70 photo of an empty beach at sunset, faded warm colors, soft vignette, slight light leak in the top right corner"

**You'll know it worked when** the white border has a faint warm tone and the corners of the image are slightly darker than the center.

## Step 4 — Specify the white frame

The white border is iconic, but it can look like a generic frame if you don't describe it. Real Polaroid borders have texture, color, and sometimes writing.

**What to type**: Mention the border details. Phrases like "white Polaroid border with subtle yellowing," "Instax Mini frame with rounded edges," "Polaroid border with handwritten caption underneath," or "slightly off-white border with a faint thumbprint" all help. If you want a caption area, ask for it explicitly: "white border with space for a handwritten date underneath."

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Instax Mini photo of a coffee cup on a wooden table, white border with subtle yellowing, slightly faded colors, morning light"

**You'll know it worked when** the border looks like aged paper rather than a Photoshop rectangle.

## Step 5 — Use the right shape

Polaroids aren't square in the same way Instagram is. Real Polaroid prints have specific **aspect ratios** — the proportions of width to height, basically the shape of the image. A standard Polaroid 600 print is slightly taller than wide. Instax Mini prints are nearly square.

**What to type**: Set the aspect ratio if your tool lets you. In Midjourney, that's the `--ar` parameter, which is the part of a prompt where you set the shape: `--ar 3:4` for a Polaroid 600, `--ar 1:1` for an Instax Mini. In other tools, look for a "size," "ratio," or "dimensions" setting before you generate.

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Polaroid 600 film photo of a vintage bicycle leaning against a brick wall, soft afternoon light, faded warm tones, slight vignette" with aspect ratio set to 3:4

**You'll know it worked when** the image proportions feel like a real instant print, not a phone screenshot.

## Step 6 — Iterate, don't restart

Your first prompt will rarely be perfect. Real Polaroid photography involved waiting for the print to develop, watching colors shift as the chemicals settled. AI generation works the same way — you'll tweak.

After your first generation, look for what feels wrong. Too sharp? Add "soft focus" or "slight motion blur." Too colorful? Add "desaturated" or "muted colors." Too clean? Add another imperfection like "slight dust on the lens." Most tools let you "vary" or "regenerate" a result, which keeps your prompt and produces a new image. Use that button often.

**💬 Example line you can copy:**
> "Polaroid SX-70 photo of a child blowing out birthday candles, soft indoor tungsten light, slightly underexposed, warm faded tones, soft vignette, white border with handwritten 'Happy 7th' below"

## Common mistakes

- **Only writing "Polaroid photo"** and stopping there. The AI needs the camera model, the lighting, and the film behavior to make it convincing.
- **Asking for too many imperfections**. Light leak + thumbprint + heavy vignette + color shift + dust + smudge all at once creates a mess. Pick two or three.
- **Forgetting the lighting**. Polaroid film reacts to light in specific ways. Without a lighting phrase, you'll get generic studio lighting every time.
- **Setting a square aspect ratio for a Polaroid 600**. Most Polaroids are slightly taller than wide. Square works for Instax Mini, not for 600.
- **Expecting one try**. Plan to generate three or four versions and pick the best. The first attempt is rarely the keeper.

## What this means for you

- **If you want quick creative fun**: Start with Step 1 and Step 3. Naming the camera and adding two imperfections will get you 80% of the way there in one prompt.
- **If you're making content for social media or a blog**: Add Step 4 (caption border) and Step 5 (correct aspect ratio) so your images feel like real prints, not framed photos.
- **If you want to learn prompt writing more broadly**: This is a useful exercise in general. Most "looks like X" prompts fail because they describe the result instead of the process. The camera, the film, the light, and the imperfections — that's the process.

## Wrap-up

A convincing AI Polaroid isn't about a white rectangle. It's about telling the AI the *story* of the photo: which camera, which film, what light, what mood. Five short additions to your prompt — camera name, lighting phrase, two imperfections, border detail, and the right aspect ratio — turn "white frame around a sharp photo" into something that actually feels like film.

Try this today: take any photo you'd normally generate, then add the camera name, one lighting phrase, and one imperfection. Generate four versions and pick the one that feels most like a memory.
